subject: geography
title: Urbanisation & Push/Pull Factors
welcome_lead: More people now live in cities than countryside. Why do millions move? Let's explore push and pull factors.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on urbanisation and push/pull factors.
final_note: Great job! You can now explain why people move to cities.

concepts.def: Growth of cities as people move from rural areas.
Reason that makes people leave their home.
Reason that attracts people to a new place.
Built-up city areas with many people.
Poor, overcrowded part of a city.

walkthroughs.body_html: People leave rural areas because of poverty, poor jobs, drought, war or few schools. These are push factors.
Cities offer jobs, schools, hospitals and electricity. These pull people to migrate.
When cities grow too fast, slums form. Examples include Dharavi in Mumbai and Kibera in Nairobi.

mcqs.q: In a tropical rainforest nutrient cycle, where is most of the nutrient stored?
options: Correlation and causation are the same thing.
Most nutrients in a rainforest are stored in the soil — that's why plants grow so well.
Most rainforest nutrients are stored in animals.
In the biomass (living plants). Litter is rapidly decomposed by warm humid conditions, and soil is leached — so cycling between biomass and litter dominates.

mcqs.q: What is a positive climate feedback loop?
options: A process where warming triggers changes that cause more warming — e.g. melting Arctic ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more heat, melting more ice (ice-albedo feedback).
Positive feedback means a good outcome for the climate.
Positive feedback means the climate balances itself out.
Most rainforest nutrients are stored in animals.

mcqs.q: Why does correlation not imply causation in geographical data?
options: Two variables may correlate because of a third confounding factor, coincidence, or reverse causation — statistical association alone does not prove one causes the other.
Positive feedback means the climate balances itself out.
Correlation and causation are the same thing.
If two variables correlate strongly, one must cause the other.
